speaker: Luke Alvezio
main_topic: Assembling agent teams to solve complex software engineering problems, specifically focusing on the 'Missions' framework developed by Factory to enable autonomous, multi-day agent workflows.

key_claims.claim: The bottleneck in software engineering is no longer intelligence, but human attention.
key_claims.support: Best engineers have backlogs of 50 features but can only drive a few forward per day because each task requires attention and review. Models are smart enough to build all 50, but lack human supervision bandwidth.

key_claims.claim: Current multi-agent frameworks are a mess, with varying terminology and opinions.
key_claims.support: Luke proposes a five-strategy taxonomy to clarify the landscape: Delegation, Creator-Verifier, Direct Communication, Negotiation, and Broadcast.

key_claims.claim: Validation must be independent of implementation to avoid the system drifting.
key_claims.support: Tests written after implementation don't catch bugs; they confirm decisions. Factory's system writes a 'validation contract' during planning, before any code is written, which can include hundreds of assertions.

key_claims.claim: Validation in a multi-day agent system must be adversarial.
key_claims.support: Neither the Scrutiny Validator nor the User-Testing Validator sees the code before verifying it. They are not invested in the implementation.

key_claims.claim: Serial execution of features is better than parallel execution for software development tasks.
key_claims.support: Parallelism leads to agents conflicting, stepping on each other's changes, duplicating work, and making inconsistent architectural decisions. Serial execution (with targeted internal parallelization for read-only tasks) reduces error rates.

key_claims.claim: A model-agnostic architecture provides a compounding advantage.
key_claims.support: Different models excel at different roles (e.g., planning vs. implementation vs. validation). Being locked into one provider restricts the system to that family's weakest capability.

key_claims.claim: The 'Missions' system is designed to improve automatically as underlying models improve.
key_claims.support: Most orchestration logic is defined in prompts and skills rather than hardcoded state machines, and worker behavior is driven by skills defined per-mission. Only bookkeeping (validation triggering, blocking progress) is deterministic.

key_claims.claim: The primary bottleneck in software engineering is no longer intelligence, but human attention.
key_claims.details: Engineers have large backlogs (e.g., 50 features) but can only advance a few per day because each step requires their supervision. Current AI models are intelligent enough to handle the entire backlog, but are limited by the need for human oversight.

key_claims.claim: A mission is an ecosystem of agents, not a single agent session.
key_claims.details: Missions consist of multiple specialized agents (Orchestrator, Workers, Validators) that coordinate through structured handoffs and a shared state to complete complex, long-running tasks.

key_claims.claim: Serial execution of features beats parallel execution for complex software development.
key_claims.details: Parallel execution leads to agent conflicts, duplicated work, and inconsistent architecture, where the coordination overhead negates speed gains. A serial approach, where features are built sequentially, ensures correctness, which compounds over multi-day runs.

key_claims.claim: The 'Missions' architecture is designed to improve as AI models improve, without requiring code changes.
key_claims.details: Almost all orchestration logic (feature decomposition, failure handling) is defined in prompts and skills, not hardcoded. This means when a new, better model is released, the system's performance naturally improves by simply swapping the model.

frameworks.name: Five Multi-Agent Strategies
components: Delegation: One agent spawns another for a subtask (e.g., sub-agents encoding tools).
Creator-Verifier: One agent builds, a different agent checks (separates concerns, removes sunk-cost bias).
Direct Communication: Agents talk peer-to-peer without a coordinator (hard to get right, no single source of truth).
Negotiation: Agents coordinate over shared resources (best for win-win situations, non-adversarial).
Broadcast: One agent sends status updates to many (critical for coherence over long tasks).

frameworks.name: Missions (Factory's System)
components: Orchestrator: Handles planning, acts as a sounding board, defines features, milestones, and the validation contract.
Workers: Handle implementation; get clean context per feature, implement, and commit via git.

Validators: Handle verification using an adversarial approach; includes Scrutiny Validator (tests, linting, code review) and User-Testing Validator (acts like a QA engineer, interacts with the app end-to-end).

frameworks.name: Structured Handoffs
components: What was implemented
What was left undone
Commands run + exit codes
Issues discovered
Whether procedures were followed

frameworks.name: Five Multi-Agent Strategies Taxonomy
frameworks.description: A classification of five primary strategies for how multiple AI agents can interact.
components: Delegation: One agent spawns another for a subtask.
Creator-Verifier: One agent builds, and a separate, unbiased agent checks the work.
Direct Communication: Peer-to-peer agent communication without a central coordinator.
Negotiation: Agents coordinate over shared resources to find a win-win outcome.
Broadcast: One agent sends status updates and shared context to many agents to maintain coherence.

frameworks.name: Missions Workflow
frameworks.description: A system that combines the multi-agent strategies into a cohesive, long-running workflow.
components: A human describes a software goal.
The system scopes the goal through a conversation with the user.
The user approves a detailed plan generated by the system.
The 'Mission' system handles the execution autonomously for hours or days.

frameworks.name: Three-Role Architecture
frameworks.description: The core architectural model for Missions, dividing responsibilities among three agent types.
components: The Orchestrator: Handles high-level planning, breaks down the goal into features and milestones, and creates the 'Validation Contract'.
Workers: Implement individual features with fresh context for each task. They commit code via git and create a structured handoff report upon completion.

Validators: Perform adversarial verification. They have never seen the code before and check its correctness against the Validation Contract. There are two types: Scrutiny Validator (static analysis, code review) and User-Testing Validator (end-to-end behavioral testing).

frameworks.name: The Validation Loop
frameworks.description: A core process in Missions to ensure correctness and prevent drift.
components: Planning Phase: An upfront 'Validation Contract' is written by the Orchestrator, defining 'done' before any code is written, independent of implementation.
After each milestone: A 'Scrutiny Validator' runs static checks (tests, linting, code review) and a 'User-Testing Validator' performs dynamic, end-to-end behavioral tests like a QA engineer.

examples.lesson: Demonstrated that validation rarely succeeds on the first try (requiring follow-up features) and that 60% of time and tokens were spent on implementation. It resulted in 50% of the final codebase being tests, with 90% test coverage.
Missions are being used to prototype new ideas overnight, build internal tools rapidly, run huge refactors/migrations, and modernize codebases.

Missions are used for practical enterprise tasks such as prototyping new features overnight, building internal tools, performing large-scale code refactors and migrations, and modernizing legacy codebases to make them more 'agent-ready'.

terminology.definition: Factory's system that combines delegation, creator-verifier, broadcast, and negotiation into a single workflow for multi-day autonomous software development.
A set of assertions written by the orchestrator during planning, before any code is written, defining what 'done' means independently of implementation.
A validator that runs tests, typechecking, and linting, and spawns dedicated code review agents.
A validator that acts like a QA engineer, spawning the application and interacting with it via computer-use to verify end-to-end functional flows.
The skill of mentally modeling how different LLMs interact, where they fail, how failures compound, and selecting the right model for specific roles in an agent ecosystem.
Groups of multiple, often specialized, AI agents collaborating to solve a problem that is too complex for a single agent.
Detailed reports generated by worker agents after completing a task to ensure context is passed coherently to subsequent agents in a long-running process.

takeaways.takeaway: To build multi-day autonomous agent systems, validation must be independent, adversarial, and behavioral (end-to-end).
Maintaining context across long-running tasks requires agents to explicitly document handoffs (what was done, what failed, exit codes) rather than relying on memory.
Serial execution of development tasks, combined with parallelization of read-only research tasks, is more effective than fully parallel execution.
Using the right model for each specific role (planning vs. coding vs. validating) creates a compounding advantage over relying on a single model family.

takeaways: Multi-agent systems can solve problems that are orders of magnitude more complex than what single agents can handle.
The key to successful long-running agentic systems is not just intelligence, but a structured architecture that ensures discipline, correctness, and coherence.
A model-agnostic architecture, where logic is in prompts rather than hard-coded, is crucial for future-proofing systems against rapid model improvements.
Effective validation must be adversarial, separating the implementation agent from the verification agent to avoid confirmation bias and catch real bugs.
For software development, a serial execution of features combined with targeted parallelism for non-conflicting sub-tasks (like research) is more effective than full parallelism.
